title: Civil Society Organisations: Economic Growth and Skills for Young People

speakers.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
speakers.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: To ask His Majesty’s Government what plans they have to involve civil society organisations in boosting economic growth and developing skills for young people.
contributions.name: Baroness Pitkeathley

contributions.text: My Lords, I beg leave to ask the Question standing in my name on the Order Paper. In doing so, I declare an interest as former president of the National Council for Voluntary Organisations.
contributions.name: Baroness Pitkeathley

contributions.who: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions (Baroness Smith of Malvern) (Lab)
contributions.text: My Lords, civil society is an important partner in delivering opportunity and growth. Through the civil society covenant, we are strengthening collaboration between government and the sector, nationally and locally. We are putting this into practice through Youth Matters, the enrichment framework and Skills England’s employability skills framework, working with civil society organisations to help young people build skills, confidence and connections to education, training and employment.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, I thank my noble friend for that reply. Civil society is a significant contributor to the development of skills, economic growth and employment, although its contribution is often overlooked. Will the Government consider Alan Milburn’s recommendation that charities and other non-profit organisations should be eligible to operate youth opportunity services where they can meet the required standards? Would the Minister perhaps be willing to meet the NCVO and other civil society organisations to discuss ways in which civil society can play a greater role in supporting and helping to grow the economy?
contributions.name: Baroness Pitkeathley

contributions.text: My Lords, certainly my noble friend does sterling work to make sure that civil society is not overlooked. We have committed to take forward Alan Milburn’s recommendation for a new locally led youth service, bringing employment, skills, health and wider support together around young people. Civil society has an important role to play, and we will of course consider how charities and other non-profit organisations can contribute as we develop the detailed delivery model for the new service. In doing that, I would be happy to meet the NCVO and other civil society organisations, as my noble friend asked.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, for the last 25 years I have worked around charities and youth services. In my experience, the best-placed people are from local youth clubs and TARAs, which employ staff from within those communities. They are often the ones who are successful in reaching those hard-to-reach young people who are not in education, employment or training. How are we going to ensure that those small organisations, which often get only one or two years’ grant aid, are supported in delivering what Milburn identified as very important last week?
contributions.name: Lord Mohammed of Tinsley

contributions.text: The noble Lord is right. I had the opportunity recently in Colchester to see a partnership between the local youth service and a voluntary sector organisation bringing young people back into the workplace, particularly through supporting their English and maths. It is a pretty constant—and understandable—refrain from civil society to have longer term funding arrangements. But in this area, we want to look at how we can support civil society to play that really important role in helping to upskill and build the confidence of young people, and to enable them to re-enter the labour market.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, charities are the lifeblood of our local communities. The Charities Aid Foundation’s annual charity insights report, published last week, reveals how charities are being forced to ration vital front-line services in the face of rising costs, falling funding and growing demand. Can the Minister reassure me that the Government will look seriously at the reforms that CAF and the sector more widely are calling for in response to these challenges?
contributions.name: Baroness Sater

contributions.text: Over the last 10 to 15 years, civil society certainly has suffered from some of the impacts of austerity, for example. That is why this Government have already taken action in a range of ways: lifting some of the burdens from the Charity Commission, which is estimated to have given back approximately £47 million to those charities; launching the local covenant partnerships programme with £11.5 million of investment to support civil society organisations so they can collaborate more effectively with local authorities and public service providers in those 15 areas; and supporting, with investment through the civil society covenant, civil society organisations to better enter into competitions and tendering in public sector supply chains. All those things are helping civil society to play its crucial role in delivering for young people.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, in the Diocese of Gloucester, the Spear programme, based at Trinity Church Cheltenham, works with 16 to 24 year-olds who are not in education, employment or training. Nationally, more than 75% of participants who have taken part in Spear programmes in the last year are still in work or education. So how will the Government ensure that churches and faith-based groups are treated as equal partners in supporting young people into work and training?
contributions.name: The Lord Bishop of Gloucester

contributions.text: This is a very good example of what I was talking about earlier. There are already very important schemes out there being run by civil society organisations of all sizes. The youth opportunity service’s being based in the local area and the knowledge it will therefore have of good-quality schemes such as the Spear scheme will enable all those resources to be brought together to support opportunity for young people.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, I declare my interest as president of the national military cadets. Does the Minister agree that the national cadet movement, be it the Royal Navy, the Royal Marines, the Army, the Air Force, or the Combined Cadet Force, plays a vital role in helping young people develop the skills we need and to build their resilience?
contributions.name: Lord Peach

contributions.text: I strongly agree with the noble and gallant Lord. I have no doubt that engaging in the cadets helps young people to learn how to work together, builds their confidence, gives them the skills that will help them throughout their lives, and certainly makes them more attractive to employers and more confident about taking up opportunities that come to them.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, we are all concerned about the number of NEETs and how to help young people. But since the Government’s national insurance rise, a third of the charities surveyed by the Charity Finance Group have made staff redundant, and the National Youth Agency has found that the share of youth workers in permanent jobs has fallen to 67%. Last Tuesday, the Government endorsed Alan Milburn’s report, which we welcome, and the calls for every major labour market decision to be tested against its effect on young people. But on Friday, they agreed to let 100,000 young Europeans come to live and work here for up to three years. Did they carry out the test recommended by Alan Milburn before they signed that agreement, and if not, how do they explain such a contradictory act?
contributions.name: Baroness Cash

contributions.text: As I am sure we will hear in the Statement following Questions, that agreement will bring considerable benefit to the UK. It will help to put right the bungled Brexit deal that was inherited from the last Government, and in doing so will benefit not just young people but the whole country.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, I welcome the work the Government are doing with the voluntary sector through the covenant. However, I am concerned about the real challenges faced by the infrastructure bodies in the voluntary sector. For example, on 1 September Reach Volunteering announced that it was closing after 45 years, and the Directory of Social Change also announced that it is going into insolvency. What more can the Government do to ensure that we make the most of the commitment of the sector to work with government and drive forward positive outcomes for young people?
contributions.name: Baroness Morgan of Drefelin

contributions.text: I understand the concerns expressed by my noble friend about the infrastructure organisations, and that was the thinking behind the setting up of the civil society covenant. It is the reason why civil society organisations have a direct route to government, through the Civil Society Council, to represent concerns about their own existence and health, as well as to inform the development of policy. They were able to do that at the most recent meeting, where, for example, youth unemployment was one of the issues discussed. I have already outlined some of the ways the Government are supporting the funding position of civil society organisations, and I know it is something that colleagues across government will continue to think hard about.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions

contributions.text: My Lords, poor numeracy is both impacting economic growth and holding young people back. The recent evaluation of Multiply indicated the importance of civil society organisations, charities and community organisations in supporting young people who have been failed by formal education. Of course, this country now has no adult numeracy programme. Will the Government commit to working with the civil sector to re-establish a programme that has all benefits that Multiply brought?
contributions.name: Baroness Bull

contributions.text: We are certainly looking hard at the evaluation of Multiply to learn the wider lessons. The adult skills fund, through its support of tailored learning, is already often supporting organisations that would not come under the heading of traditional education providers to reach out and engage with people in order to get them closer to the labour market and to develop the skills that are crucial for their success.
contributions.name: Baroness Smith of Malvern
contributions.role: The Minister of State, Department for Education and Department for Work and Pensions
